rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical separations while limiting the risk of non-elution. The midpoint temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to probe selectivity within the crowded four-peak cluster and the late critical pair. All peaks currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving room for subsequent gradient flattening if needed.
Probe the low-temperature end with the same gradient to assess whether it improves selectivity in the crowded regions. This completes a broad temperature screen before adjusting gradient slope.

Flatten the gradient at the best temperature to test whether slope-dependent selectivity opens the remaining close pair and resolves the pair at R 1.40. The current 7.23-minute last peak provides some room to improve separation before incurring a time penalty.
Shorten the fully resolving gradient by one grid step to bring the last peak below 10 minutes. This tests whether the critical pair retains R ≥ 1.5 and achieves the maximum CRF.

Shift the fully resolving gradient upward by 0.05 organic fraction while preserving its slope. This should advance elution toward the 10-minute target while testing whether the critical separation is maintained.

Slightly flatten the best gradient by lowering phi1 one grid step to improve the sole unresolved pair. The 0.75-minute margin before the time penalty should accommodate this change and may allow CRF 1.000.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; now test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten elution while retaining full resolution. Keeping phi1 fixed also slightly flattens the gradient, which may offset the critical-pair resolution loss seen when shifting both endpoints upward.
Lower phi1 one step to recover the small resolution deficit while retaining the earlier elution gained from phi0 0.20. This may match the maximum CRF with a shorter elution window than injection 7.

Test a narrower, higher-starting gradient to advance elution while preserving the maximum score. The shallower slope is intended to compensate for the critical-pair resolution lost when increasing the starting organic fraction.

Raise temperature one step from the shortest fully resolved method to test whether elution can be accelerated without losing CRF 1.000. Monitor both the central critical pair and the temperature-sensitive late separations.

Test a lower starting organic fraction with a moderately steeper slope at 30 C to rebalance the central and late critical separations. This explores a route to full resolution near the faster eight-minute elution window, while retaining the established CRF 1.000 methods as fallbacks.

Return to the temperature that consistently gives full resolution and test a higher-starting, shallower gradient. The reduced slope is intended to protect the central critical pair while seeking a shorter fully resolved elution window.

Probe a larger temperature shift with the narrowed gradient to see whether selectivity improves beyond the near-coelution encountered at 30 C. The maximum CRF is already secured, so this tests an alternative route to faster full resolution.

Increase temperature one step to test whether the two deficient central separations open after the order changes seen between 30 and 40 C. The last peak at 7.08 minutes leaves ample time margin for subsequent slope adjustments if needed.

Flatten the gradient at 45 C to test whether the three moderately deficient pairs can reach full resolution. The current last peak at 6.72 minutes provides room to trade speed for separation while staying below the time-penalty threshold.

Return to the near-optimal 30 C method and shorten its gradient one step to test whether the late critical pair improves with a steeper slope. The central pairs are near the resolution threshold, so this directly checks the tradeoff between their separation and faster elution.

Test a slope between injections 8 and 9, bracketing the transition to full resolution at phi0 0.20. This targets CRF 1.000 with slightly earlier final elution than the currently fastest fully resolved method.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction moves the central critical pair through its selectivity crossover into a faster, resolved elution order. Previously established CRF 1.000 methods remain the benchmarks if this more aggressive compression loses resolution.
Shorten the fastest fully resolved gradient by one grid step. The minimum resolution of 1.88 provides some margin to accelerate elution while retaining CRF 1.000.

Test a further gradient shortening, since the minimum resolution improved at 14 minutes and all pairs retain margin. Monitor the late pair and the central separation at R 2.92, which decreased as the gradient steepened.
Shorten the gradient one more grid step to seek faster elution at CRF 1.000. The declining central and late separations are now the likely limits, so this tests the boundary of full resolution.

Shorten by one grid step to establish the speed limit for this gradient window. The central and late critical pairs may fall below 1.5; if so, injection 22 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.

Return to the resolving eight-minute duration and test a higher starting organic fraction for faster elution. Lowering phi1 also flattens the slope to help protect the central and late critical pairs; injection 22 remains the fastest proven fallback.

Use the final injection to flatten the high-starting gradient and recover its sole deficient central separation, while retaining early elution. CRF 1.000 is already secured, with injection 22 remaining the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.
